docs.title: Initial setup
docs.text:
Initial setup

The same setup as a diagram of how data flows:

flowchart LR
    DCM["1. DC main<br/>read-write"] -->|"2. WAL"| DCO["3. DC object storage"]
    DCO -->|"4. recover"| DCS["5. DC standby<br/>read-only"]
    DCO <-->|"6. replicate both ways"| DRO["7. DR object storage"]
    DRO -->|"8. recover"| DRM["9. DR main<br/>read-only"]
    DRO -->|"10. recover"| DRS["11. DR standby<br/>read-only"]

    classDef step fill:#7986cb26,stroke:#7986cb,stroke-width:2px
    classDef ok fill:#43a04726,stroke:#43a047,stroke-width:2px
    classDef opt fill:#9575cd26,stroke:#9575cd,stroke-width:2px
    class DCO,DRO step
    class DCM ok
    class DCS,DRM,DRS opt
  • One keenPGO operator is on top and manages everything.
  • DC and DR are two different Kubernetes clusters.
  • Each site has two database clusters:
Cluster What it is Main cluster Primary and replica pods. DC main is in namespace demo-dc, DR main is in namespace demo-dr. Standby cluster One pod, read only, in its own namespace. It always recovers from the object storage of its own site.
  • Each site has its own object storage.
  • The two object storages replicate both ways (like master - master).
  • DC main cluster is the only one that takes writes. It pushes WAL files to DC object storage.
  • DC standby cluster recovers from DC object storage.
  • The WAL is copied to DR object storage. DR main cluster and DR standby cluster both recover from it.
  • DR main cluster has the same number of pods as DC main, but it is read only.

docs.title: Why we need a standby cluster
docs.text:
• HA inside one site (primary + replicas) only saves us when a pod or a node fails.
  • If the full DC goes down (power, network, storage or Kubernetes problem), all pods go down together.
  • The standby cluster has a full copy of the data, kept up to date from object storage.
  • It is already running and replaying WAL, so we can promote in minutes. Restore from backup can take hours for a big database.
  • Data loss is small, because WAL is shipped all the time, not once a day.
  • Standby is read only, so nobody can write on it by mistake.
  • During the drill, when the DC main cluster is shut down, the DC standby cluster still keeps a live copy of the data on the DC side.
  • Before we switch back, we check the data on the DC standby cluster.
  • We can run reports and read-only queries on a standby.

Standby cluster is not a backup

If someone drops a table on the main cluster, it is dropped on all standbys also. For this we still need backups and point-in-time restore.

docs.title: Which main cluster is active
docs.text:
The standby setting in the main cluster decides which site is active.

State DC main standby.enabled DR main standby.enabled Apps write to Normal (DC active) false true DC main DR active true (and shut down) false DR main

The standby clusters on both sites always have standby.enabled: true.

When DC is active, the DC main kustomize file has:

DC main kustomize file
spec:
  standby:
    enabled: false

And the DR main kustomize file has:

DR main kustomize file
spec:
  standby:
    enabled: true
    repoName: <repo that points at DR object storage>

Only one main cluster can have standby.enabled: false

If both main clusters are primary at the same time, both take writes and the data becomes different on both sides (split brain). So we always shut down the old main cluster first, and only then promote the other one.

docs.title: DR drill: switch from DC to DR
docs.text:
Do these steps one by one

Do not skip any step.

The six steps from DC to DR:

flowchart LR
    A["1. Stop apps"] --> B["2. Close connections,<br/>switch WAL"] --> C["3. Shut down<br/>DC main"] --> D["4. Check sync,<br/>shut down DR main"] --> E["5. Promote and<br/>start DR main"] --> F["6. Apps to DR"]

    classDef step fill:#7986cb26,stroke:#7986cb,stroke-width:2px
    classDef ok fill:#43a04726,stroke:#43a047,stroke-width:2px
    class A,B,C,D,E step
    class F ok

docs.title: Step 1: Shut down the application
docs.text:
Stop all applications that connect to the DC main cluster. Scale the app deployments to 0, or stop them in the way your team does it.

Stop the application
kubectl scale deployment <app-deployment> -n <app-namespace> --replicas=0

If you use pgBouncer, stop it also, so no new connection comes.

docs.title: Step 2: Check connections, close them, then switch WAL
docs.text:
Find the primary pod of the DC main cluster:

Find the primary pod
kubectl exec -it <any-db-pod> -n demo-dc -- patronictl list

The pod with role Leader is the primary.

Connect to the primary:

Connect to the DC primary
kubectl exec -it <dc-primary-pod> -n demo-dc -- psql -U postgres

Check who is still connected:

Check connections
SELECT pid, usename, datname, client_addr, application_name, state
FROM pg_stat_activity
WHERE backend_type = 'client backend'
  AND pid <> pg_backend_pid();

If any app connection is still there, close it:

Close connections
SELECT pg_terminate_backend(pid)
FROM pg_stat_activity
WHERE backend_type = 'client backend'
  AND pid <> pg_backend_pid();

Add one test row, so we can check later that DR has all the data:

Add a test row
CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS dr_drill_check (checked_at timestamptz, note text);
INSERT INTO dr_drill_check VALUES (now(), 'before DC shutdown');

Now take a checkpoint and switch WAL, so the last WAL file goes to object storage:

Checkpoint and switch WAL
CHECKPOINT;
SELECT pg_switch_wal();
SELECT pg_current_wal_lsn();

Write down the LSN

Write down the LSN from the last command. We need it in step 4.

Check that the WAL is archived and there is no failure:

Check WAL archiving
SELECT last_archived_wal, last_archived_time, failed_count, last_failed_wal
FROM pg_stat_archiver;

last_archived_time should be just now.

Archiving failures

If failed_count goes up, stop here and fix archiving first.

docs.title: Step 3: Shut down the DC main cluster
docs.text:
Shut down DC main
kubectl patch keenpgcluster/demo-dc-db-pod -n demo-dc --type merge --patch '{"spec":{"shutdown": true}}'
Expected output
keenpgcluster.<api-group>/demo-dc-db-pod patched

Check that the database pods are gone:

Check the pods
kubectl get pods -n demo-dc

Expected output (no database pods; backup or other helper pods can still be there):

Expected output
No resources found in demo-dc namespace.

Now, for safety, set DC main to standby in the DC main kustomize file. So if somebody starts it by mistake, it comes up read only, not as a second primary.

DC main kustomize file
spec:
  standby:
    enabled: true
    repoName: <repo that points at DC object storage>
Apply the kustomize
kubectl apply -k <dc-main-kustomize-path>
Expected output
keenpgcluster.<api-group>/demo-dc-db-pod configured

Do not touch the DC standby cluster

It keeps running and recovering from DC object storage.

docs.title: Step 4: Check sync on DR, then shut down the DR main cluster
docs.text:
First check that the DR main cluster has all the data from DC.

Connect to the DR main standby leader:

Find the standby leader and connect
kubectl exec -it <any-db-pod> -n demo-dr -- patronictl list
kubectl exec -it <dr-standby-leader-pod> -n demo-dr -- psql -U postgres

Check that it is still a standby:

Check recovery mode
SELECT pg_is_in_recovery();

It should say t.

Check how much WAL is replayed:

Check WAL replay
SELECT pg_last_wal_replay_lsn(), pg_last_xact_replay_timestamp();
SELECT pg_wal_lsn_diff('<lsn-from-step-2>', pg_last_wal_replay_lsn());

The second query should give 0 or a negative number. If it gives a positive number, DR is still behind. Wait and check again.

Check the test row:

Check the test row
SELECT * FROM dr_drill_check ORDER BY checked_at DESC LIMIT 1;

You should see the row before DC shutdown. You can run the same checks on the DC standby cluster and the DR standby cluster also.

When sync is OK, shut down the DR main cluster before promotion:

Shut down DR main
kubectl patch keenpgcluster/demo-dr-db-pod -n demo-dr --type merge --patch '{"spec":{"shutdown": true}}'
Expected output
keenpgcluster.<api-group>/demo-dr-db-pod patched

Now both main clusters are down. Nobody can write. Only the two standby clusters are running.

Switch to DR: main clusters shut down

docs.title: Step 5: Promote DR main and start it
docs.text:
Set standby to false in the DR main kustomize file:

DR main kustomize file
spec:
  standby:
    enabled: false

Apply the kustomize:

Apply the kustomize
kubectl apply -k <dr-main-kustomize-path>
Expected output
keenpgcluster.<api-group>/demo-dr-db-pod configured

Start the DR main cluster:

Start DR main
kubectl patch keenpgcluster/demo-dr-db-pod -n demo-dr --type merge --patch '{"spec":{"shutdown": false}}'
Expected output
keenpgcluster.<api-group>/demo-dr-db-pod patched

Watch the pods come up:

Watch the pods
kubectl get pods -n demo-dr --watch

Check that DR main is now primary:

Check the role
kubectl exec -it <any-db-pod> -n demo-dr -- patronictl list

One pod should have role Leader (not Standby Leader). In psql, SELECT pg_is_in_recovery(); should now say f.

docs.title: Step 6: Point the apps to DR and start them
docs.text:
• Change the DNS or connection string to the DR main primary service.
  • Start the apps and pgBouncer.
  • Do a small write test and check the app is working.
  • Check that new WAL and backups go to DR object storage.

This is how it looks now:

DR active

  • DR main cluster is primary and pushes WAL to DR object storage.
  • DR standby cluster recovers from DR object storage.
  • DC main cluster is shut down.
  • On the DC side only the DC standby cluster (1 pod) is running. It recovers DR WAL from DC object storage, which comes by the both-way replication.

docs.title: DR drill: switch back from DR to DC
docs.text:
We use the same method, only the sites are opposite.

The seven steps from DR back to DC:

docs.title: Step 1: Shut down the application
docs.text:
Stop all apps and pgBouncer that connect to the DR main cluster.

Stop the application
kubectl scale deployment <app-deployment> -n <app-namespace> --replicas=0

docs.title: Step 2: Check connections, close them, then switch WAL
docs.text:
Connect to the DR main primary:

Connect to the DR primary
kubectl exec -it <dr-primary-pod> -n demo-dr -- psql -U postgres

Close any open app connection (same queries as before):

Close connections
SELECT pg_terminate_backend(pid)
FROM pg_stat_activity
WHERE backend_type = 'client backend'
  AND pid <> pg_backend_pid();

Add the test row, switch WAL and note the LSN:

Test row, switch WAL, note the LSN
INSERT INTO dr_drill_check VALUES (now(), 'before DR shutdown');
CHECKPOINT;
SELECT pg_switch_wal();
SELECT pg_current_wal_lsn();
SELECT last_archived_wal, last_archived_time, failed_count FROM pg_stat_archiver;

docs.title: Step 3: Shut down the DR main cluster
docs.text:
Shut down DR main
kubectl patch keenpgcluster/demo-dr-db-pod -n demo-dr --type merge --patch '{"spec":{"shutdown": true}}'
Expected output
keenpgcluster.<api-group>/demo-dr-db-pod patched

For safety, set DR main back to standby in the DR main kustomize file and apply it:

DR main kustomize file
spec:
  standby:
    enabled: true
    repoName: <repo that points at DR object storage>
Apply the kustomize
kubectl apply -k <dr-main-kustomize-path>

docs.title: Step 4: Check sync on the DC standby cluster, then shut it down
docs.text:
Do not start the DC main cluster

It stays shut down. We come back on the DC standby cluster, because it was running the whole time and has the latest data.

Switch back to DC: DR main shut down

Connect to the DC standby cluster:

Connect to the DC standby
kubectl exec -it <dc-standby-pod> -n <dc-standby-namespace> -- psql -U postgres

Check the data:

Check the data
SELECT pg_is_in_recovery();
SELECT pg_wal_lsn_diff('<lsn-from-step-2>', pg_last_wal_replay_lsn());
SELECT * FROM dr_drill_check ORDER BY checked_at DESC LIMIT 1;
Check Expected result pg_is_in_recovery() t LSN diff 0 or negative Test row before DR shutdown

Also check the logs for any WAL or timeline error:

Check the logs
kubectl logs <dc-standby-pod> -n <dc-standby-namespace> --tail=100

When everything is OK, shut down the DC standby cluster before promotion:

Shut down the DC standby
kubectl patch keenpgcluster/<dc-standby-cluster> -n <dc-standby-namespace> --type merge --patch '{"spec":{"shutdown": true}}'
Expected output
keenpgcluster.<api-group>/<dc-standby-cluster> patched

docs.title: Step 5: Promote the DC standby cluster and start it
docs.text:
In the DC standby kustomize file set standby to false:

DC standby kustomize file
spec:
  standby:
    enabled: false

Apply the kustomize:

Apply the kustomize
kubectl apply -k <dc-standby-kustomize-path>
Expected output
keenpgcluster.<api-group>/<dc-standby-cluster> configured

Start it:

Start the DC standby
kubectl patch keenpgcluster/<dc-standby-cluster> -n <dc-standby-namespace> --type merge --patch '{"spec":{"shutdown": false}}'

Check that it is now the master:

Check the role
kubectl exec -it <dc-standby-pod> -n <dc-standby-namespace> -- patronictl list

The pod should have role Leader (not Standby Leader). In psql, SELECT pg_is_in_recovery(); should now say f.

docs.title: Step 6: Point the apps to the DC standby cluster and start them
docs.text:
• Change the DNS or connection string to the primary service of the DC standby cluster.
  • Start the apps and pgBouncer, and do a small write test.
  • Check that new WAL goes to DC object storage.
  • Start DR main again. It comes up as standby, because we set standby: true in step 3:
Start DR main
kubectl patch keenpgcluster/demo-dr-db-pod -n demo-dr --type merge --patch '{"spec":{"shutdown": false}}'

This is how it looks now:

DC standby active

  • DC standby cluster is now the master. The application connects to it.
  • It pushes WAL to DC object storage.
  • DR main and DR standby recover from DR object storage.
  • DC main cluster is still shut down.

docs.title: Step 7: Recreate the DC main cluster as standby
docs.text:
Do not start the old DC main cluster as it is

The DC standby cluster is now the current master. The old DC main cluster is shut down and its data is old (it is on the old timeline). Do not start it as it is, and never set standby: false on it.

Recreate it as a standby of the current master:

  1. Keep shutdown: true on demo-dc-db-pod.
  2. Delete the old DC main cluster and its data volumes (PVCs).
  3. In the DC main kustomize file set standby.enabled: true and repoName pointing at DC object storage.
  4. Apply the kustomize and set shutdown: false.
  5. It restores from the latest backup in DC object storage and then keeps recovering WAL.
  6. Check pg_is_in_recovery() is t and the lag is small.

New roles for the next drill

Now the DC main cluster is the standby, and the DC standby cluster is the master. For the next drill, use these new roles.

docs.title: Quick reference
docs.text: Step DC → DR DR → DC 1 Stop apps on DC Stop apps on DR 2 Close connections, switch WAL on DC main Close connections, switch WAL on DR main 3 Shut down DC main, set standby: true Shut down DR main, set standby: true 4 Check sync on DR main, shut down DR main Check sync on DC standby, shut down DC standby 5 DR main standby: false, apply kustomize, start DC standby standby: false, apply kustomize, start 6 Apps → DR main Apps → DC standby, start DR main as standby 7 Recreate DC main as standby

docs.title: Why the drill can fail
docs.text:
These are the common reasons. Check them before the drill.

Problem What happens Apps are not fully stopped Some writes come after the WAL switch, and the other side misses them. WAL archiving is failing Wrong bucket keys or a full bucket. failed_count in pg_stat_archiver goes up. Object storage replication is slow or broken The last WAL file did not reach the other site yet. Standby is not replaying Wrong repoName, a missing WAL file, or the standby was already behind before the drill. We forgot standby: true on the old main cluster When it starts again, both sides are primary (split brain). Kustomize file not updated Wrong path, or the change is not saved in git, so a sync tool puts the old value back. Operator is not working The patch is accepted, but nothing happens to the pods. Pods stay Pending on the other site Not enough nodes, CPU or memory, PVC or storage class problem, or anti-affinity cannot be met. Timeline problem when coming back After DR main is promoted it starts a new timeline. If the DC standby cluster cannot follow it, it must be rebuilt from a DR backup. Old DC main started by mistake Its data is old. It must be recreated as standby, never started as primary. Users or secrets are different on the two sites Apps cannot log in after the switch. Apps still point to the old site DNS TTL is long, or pgBouncer or the app has the old address cached. Network or firewall issue A site cannot reach its object storage. Long running sessions They keep coming back, so the shutdown takes too long.

docs.title: DR checklist
docs.text:
• keenPGO operator manages all four clusters (DC main, DC standby, DR main, DR standby)
  • DC main has standby.enabled: false, all others have standby.enabled: true
  • DR main has the same number of pods as DC main, and enough nodes
  • Both object storages are working and replicate both ways
  • WAL archiving has no failures and standby lag is small
  • WAL retention is long enough to cover the full drill time
  • Kustomize paths for both main clusters are known and in git
  • App connection strings can be changed quickly
  • Drill is done in a test environment first, then in production
  • Backups and monitoring cover both sites

docs.title: Architecture overview
docs.text:
A keenPGO deployment has two layers: a control layer that manages desired state, and a data layer that serves your applications.

flowchart TB
    subgraph control["Control layer"]
        OP["keenPGO operator"]
        CR["Cluster resource (desired state)"]
        OP -- watches --> CR
    end

    subgraph data["Data layer"]
        direction LR
        P["Primary<br/>(read / write)"]
        R1["Replica 1<br/>(read only)"]
        R2["Replica 2<br/>(read only)"]
        P -- replication --> R1
        P -- replication --> R2
    end

    SVC["Primary service"]
    APP["Applications"]

    OP -- creates and updates --> data
    APP --> SVC --> P
    P -- backups and WAL --> STORE[("Backup storage")]

    style data fill:#9e9e9e1a,stroke:#9e9e9e

    class P ok
    class R1,R2 opt

docs.title: Components
docs.text: Component Role Operator Watches cluster definitions and creates, updates and repairs the resources they describe. It does not sit in the data path. Cluster resource Your declaration of what you want: PostgreSQL version, number of instances, storage, placement rules. Primary instance The one instance that accepts writes. Replica instances Continuously copy changes from the primary and can be promoted if it fails. Primary service A stable address that always points at the current primary, so applications don't need to know which pod it is. Backup storage Object or volume storage holding base backups and archived write-ahead logs.

docs.title: Design principle: the operator is not a single point of failure
docs.text:
Once a cluster is running, patroni is responsible for failover. If the operator is down:

  • Running clusters keep serving traffic
  • Failover still happens
  • Changes to cluster definitions wait until the operator returns

docs.title: What keenPGO protects against
docs.text:
Problem What happens Primary pod crashes A replica is promoted automatically Node hosting the primary fails A replica on another node is promoted A replica fails The cluster keeps running and the replica is rebuilt Operator unavailable Existing clusters keep running, as described above Planned maintenance Handled one instance at a time, see Maintenance without downtime

Limits of high availability

Replication protects against failures, not mistakes. A dropped table is dropped on every replica. Keep backups, and see disaster recovery for protection against loss of a whole site.

Availability is also bounded by the platform underneath. If Kubernetes itself or its storage layer fails, the database is affected too.

docs.title: How failover works
docs.text:

sequenceDiagram
    participant App as Application
    participant P as Primary
    participant R1 as Replica 1
    participant R2 as Replica 2

    P-xP: Primary fails
    R1->>R1: Detects missing primary
    R2->>R2: Detects missing primary
    R1->>R2: Compare replication positions
    Note over R1,R2: Replica with the most data wins
    R1->>R1: Promote to primary
    R2->>R1: Follow new primary
    App->>R1: Reconnect via primary service
Step What happens 1. Detection <How a failed primary is noticed and how long keenPGO waits before acting> 2. Selection <How the best replica is chosen, for example the most up-to-date one> 3. Promotion <How the replica becomes the primary> 4. Redirection The primary service now points at the new primary, so applications reconnect to the same address. 5. Recovery <What happens when the old primary returns: rewound, rebuilt, or rejoined as a replica>

Typical failover time: <value, and the conditions under which you measured it>.

Make applications failover-friendly

Connections drop during failover. Use a driver or connection pool that retries, set sensible connection timeouts, and keep transactions short. Done well, users never notice.

docs.text:

docs.title: Pod anti-affinity
docs.text: Anti-affinity tells Kubernetes not to put all instances of the same cluster together. Which means we highly recommend to use different node for each instance of same cluster.

docs.title: Node affinity
docs.text:
Node affinity places instances on nodes with particular labels. Typical uses:

  • Fast local storage or high-memory nodes for the primary
  • Keeping a replica in a specific nodesets
  • Isolating databases from other workloads which means dedicated nodes for DB instance in production.
Node affinity
spec:
  # <node affinity setting>

docs.title: Tolerations
docs.text:
Kubernetes Tolerations can help with the scheduling of Pods to appropriate nodes. There are many reasons that a Kubernetes administrator may want to use tolerations, such as restricting the types of Pods that can be assigned to particular Nodes. Reasoning and strategy for using taints and tolerations is outside the scope of this documentation.

Tolerations
spec:
  # <tolerations setting>

docs.title: Rolling restarts
docs.text:
Some PostgreSQL settings only apply after a restart. Restarting everything at once would cause an outage, so keenPGO works through the cluster in order:

flowchart LR
    A["Update replica 1"] --> B["Update replica 2"]
    B --> C["Controlled switchover<br/>to an updated replica"]
    C --> D["Update former primary"]
    D --> E["Done: cluster fully updated"]

    classDef step fill:#7986cb26,stroke:#7986cb,stroke-width:2px
    classDef ok fill:#43a04726,stroke:#43a047,stroke-width:2px
    class A,B,C,D step
    class E ok
  1. Each replica is stopped cleanly, updated and restarted, and must be healthy before the next one begins.
  2. The primary role is handed to an updated replica in a planned switchover.
  3. The former primary is updated and rejoins as a replica.

Applications see one short reconnect, not an outage. keenPGO starts this process automatically when it detects a change that needs a restart.

docs.title: Pod disruption budgets
docs.text:
When administrators drain nodes or upgrade Kubernetes, pods are evicted on purpose. A pod disruption budget (PDB) states how many database pods must stay available during such events.

Pod disruption budget
spec:
  # <minimum available setting>

Default behaviour: <explain the default for single-instance and multi-instance clusters>.

Warning

Don't set the minimum equal to your total instance count. Node maintenance would then be blocked indefinitely.

docs.title: Test failover before you need it
docs.text:
Run this in a test environment first.

  1. Find the current primary:

    Find the primary
    kubectl get pods -n <namespace> -l <primary-label-selector>

  2. Delete that pod to simulate a crash:

    Simulate a crash
    kubectl delete pod <primary-pod-name> -n <namespace>

  3. Watch the cluster recover:

    Watch the pods
    kubectl get pods -n <namespace> --watch

  4. Confirm that a different pod is now the primary and your application reconnected and kept working.

If something doesn't behave as expected, see troubleshooting.

docs.title: Production checklist
docs.text:
• At least three instances
  • Instances on separate nodes, ideally in separate nodes
  • Synchronous replication where data loss is unacceptable
  • A pod disruption budget below your instance count
  • Applications and connection pools retry after connection loss
  • Failover tested at least once
  • Backups configured and a restore tested
  • Monitoring alerts on replica lag and failovers
